1a.html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) is UNDP's composite index, from 0 to 1, that combines life expectancy, schooling and log GNI per capita at purchasing power parity (PPP: rates that equalise the cost of a common basket) by a geometric mean.

Strengths

  1. Broader than income. It treats health and education as ends of development (the capabilities view), not only as inputs, so it exposes "growth without development".
  2. Income is not destiny. Countries with similar incomes differ widely: in the 2018 data Bangladesh ranked 9 places higher on HDI than on GNI per capita, while Equatorial Guinea ranked 80 places lower. Health and education policy matters.
  3. Simple and comparable. Four widely available indicators rank about 190 countries on one scale, track progress, and can be computed for regions, groups, and rural and urban areas.
  4. Sensible form. Log income reflects diminishing returns to income, and the geometric mean penalises lopsided development.

Weaknesses

  1. Arbitrary weights and goalposts. Equal one-third weights on quantities in different units are a value judgement, and changing the minima or maxima changes the rankings.
  2. Averages hide distribution. A national value says nothing about inequality between rich and poor, women and men, or regions.
  3. Quantity, not quality. Years of schooling ignore what is learned; life expectancy ignores years lived in poor health.
  4. Narrow, with weak data. It omits freedom, security and the environment. Expected schooling is a forecast, and PPP incomes are estimates.

Conclusion: the HDI is a useful complement to GNI per capita, not a complete welfare measure; use it with the inequality-adjusted HDI, the Gender Inequality Index and the Multidimensional Poverty Index.
pts: Defines the HDI: life expectancy, schooling and log GNI per capita (PPP) combined into a 0 to 1 index
Strength: broader than income, health and education as ends (capabilities), exposing growth without development
Strength: HDI and income rankings differ, with an example (for example Bangladesh +9, Cuba +43, Equatorial Guinea -80)
Strength: simple, transparent and comparable across countries, over time and across regions or groups
Strength: log income for diminishing returns and a geometric mean that penalises uneven development
Weakness: equal weights and goalposts are value judgements; changing them changes the rankings
Weakness: national averages hide inequality by income, gender or region
Weakness: counts quantity not quality (schooling is not learning, life length is not healthy life)
Weakness: omits freedom, security or environment; expected schooling is a forecast and PPP data are estimates
Concludes that the HDI complements GNI rather than replacing it, used with the IHDI, GII or MPI
1a.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-21; HDR 2019 technical notes, p 2; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 90-93, 144-145
1a.watch:
• "Explain" needs a reason for each point, not a list of labels. Other sound strengths or weaknesses with a reason earn the same credit.
  • Do not call the HDI "just income again": the slides stress that income and HDI are not strongly correlated (hum-ch2 slide 21).
  • A subtler weakness: even the geometric mean still lets more income offset shorter lives, at an implicit rate that differs between rich and poor countries.
  • The rank gaps (+9, -80) are GNI rank minus HDI rank from the 2018 table in Todaro; a positive value means the HDI rank is better.

1b.html:
I would keep the HDI's three dimensions (health, knowledge, living standard) and its geometric mean, but change four things:

  1. Adjust for inequality. Report an inequality-adjusted HDI as the headline figure, because a national average hides gaps between rich and poor, women and men, and rural and urban areas.
  2. Measure quality. Use learning-adjusted years of schooling (from test scores) and healthy life expectancy, because a year in school in Mali teaches less than one in Norway, and a year confined to bed is not a year of full capability.
  3. Count achievements, not forecasts. Replace expected years of schooling, a UN projection that can be optimistic in poor countries, with school completion rates.
  4. Add a freedom or sustainability dimension. Development is the expansion of people's freedoms, and progress that depletes natural resources cannot last.

Each change must use data available for about 190 countries, or the index loses its main strength: simple comparison.
pts: A first change with its reason, for example an inequality adjustment because averages hide the distribution
A second change with its reason, for example learning-adjusted schooling or healthy life expectancy because years are not quality
A third change with its reason, for example achievements (completion) in place of forecast schooling, or a freedom or environment dimension
A fourth change or a justified choice to keep a feature, for example tested weights or keeping the geometric mean (any sound change with a reason earns the credit)
Notes the limit on redesign: indicators need comparable data for all countries, so simplicity is kept
1b.src: Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-20; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 93-94, 145
1b.watch:
• The marks go to the reasons. A list of changes with no "why" earns little.
  • UNDP already publishes the inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), the Gender Inequality Index and, since 2020, a planetary-pressures-adjusted HDI; naming them shows the proposal is workable.
  • Equal weights are another target: they are a value judgement on quantities in different units, so publishing rankings under alternative weights shows how robust they are.

2a.html:
The fundamental equation (equation of motion) of the Solow model gives the change in capital per worker. Here the labour force L is constant.

Step 1. Production function per worker. Y = F(K, L) has constant returns to scale: zY = F(zK, zL) for any z > 0. With z = 1/L:

\frac{Y}{L} = F\!\left(\frac{K}{L}, 1\right) \;\Rightarrow\; y = f(k), \qquad y = \frac{Y}{L},\; k = \frac{K}{L}

f(k) shows diminishing MPK: each extra unit of k adds less output.

Step 2. Saving and investment. With no government, y = c + i. The consumption function is c = (1 - s)y, where s is the exogenous saving rate. So saving per worker is y - c = sy, and

i = y - c = s y = s f(k)

Investment equals saving.

Step 3. Capital accumulation. Investment adds capital; depreciation, a fraction \delta of the stock each period, removes it:

\Delta K = I - \delta K

Step 4. Per worker. L is fixed, so dividing by L gives \Delta k = i - \delta k. Substituting i = s f(k):

\boxed{\Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k}

This equation determines k over time, and through k all the other variables: y = f(k), c = (1-s) f(k).

Step 5. Steady state. k is constant when investment just covers depreciation:

\Delta k = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; s f(k^*) = \delta k^*

If k < k^*, s f(k) > \delta k and k rises; if k > k^*, it falls. So k^* is stable.

Example (slides): 0.3\sqrt{k^*} = 0.1k^* gives k^* = 9, y^* = 3, c^* = 0.7 \times 3 = 2.1.
pts: Uses constant returns (z = 1/L) to write y = f(k) with y = Y/L, k = K/L
States diminishing MPK in f(k)
From y = c + i and c = (1-s)y: i = s y = s f(k) (saving equals investment)
Capital accumulation \Delta K = I - \delta K, so \Delta k = i - \delta k with L fixed
Final equation \Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k
Steady state \Delta k = 0: s f(k^*) = \delta k^*
Stability: k rises below k^* and falls above it (in words or on a diagram)
Notes that k determines the other variables: y = f(k) and c = (1-s) f(k)
2a.src: Solow model (Mankiw ch 8), slides 8-17, 24, 26-30; Mankiw, Macroeconomics, ch 8
2a.watch:
• Do not add nk here: the question excludes population growth.
  • s is the only lower-case variable that is not its capital divided by L (slide 11).
  • The steady state is a level, not a growth rate: with L and technology fixed, output stops growing once k reaches k^*.

2b.html:
Given: Y = K^{1/3} L^{2/3}; s = 0.2; \delta = 0.05; no population growth.

Find: the per-worker production function and the steady-state capital per worker k^*.

Per-worker form. The exponents add to 1 (constant returns), so divide by L:

\frac{Y}{L} = \frac{K^{1/3} L^{2/3}}{L} = \left(\frac{K}{L}\right)^{1/3} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{y = k^{1/3}}

Steady state. With \Delta k = s f(k) - \delta k = 0:

\begin{aligned} 0.2\,(k^*)^{1/3} &= 0.05\,k^* \\ (k^*)^{2/3} &= \frac{0.2}{0.05} = 4 \\ k^* &= 4^{3/2} = 8 \end{aligned}

Then y^* = 8^{1/3} = 2, i^* = 0.2 \times 2 = 0.4 = \delta k^*, c^* = 1.6.

Answer: y = k^{1/3}; k^* = 8 units of capital per worker.
pts: Notes constant returns (exponents add to 1)
Divides by L: Y/L = (K/L)^{1/3}
Per-worker production function y = k^{1/3}
Steady-state condition s f(k^*) = \delta k^* from \Delta k = 0
0.2 (k^*)^{1/3} = 0.05 k^*, so (k^*)^{2/3} = 4
k^* = 4^{3/2} = 8
2b.src: Solow model (Mankiw ch 8), slides 8, 15-17, 26-30; Mankiw, Macroeconomics, ch 8
2b.watch:
• The exponents are printed small above the line: the full-resolution scan reads K^{1/3}L^{2/3} (constant returns), even where a low-resolution copy shows only the "/3".
  • (k^*)^{2/3} = 4 gives k^* = 4^{3/2} = 8, not 4^{2/3} = 2.52.

3a.html:
All three measures compare benefits B_t and costs C_t arising in different years by discounting them to the present at a discount rate r: PV = FV/(1+r)^t (end-of-year flows, year 0 = now).

Net present value (NPV) is the difference between the present value of benefits and the present value of costs:

\mathrm{NPV} = PV(B) - PV(C) = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}

Decision: accept if \mathrm{NPV} > 0, reject if \mathrm{NPV} < 0. A positive NPV is the net value the project adds in taka today, after paying the opportunity cost of capital; \mathrm{NPV} = 0 means it earns exactly r.

Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is the present value of benefits per unit present value of costs:

\mathrm{BCR} = \frac{PV(B)}{PV(C)}

Decision: accept if \mathrm{BCR} > 1. BCR > 1 exactly when NPV > 0, so they agree on accept or reject, but BCR measures efficiency per taka while NPV measures total value.

Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV is zero:

\sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+\mathrm{IRR})^t} = 0

Decision: accept if IRR exceeds the required rate. It is found by trial: with L giving a positive NPV and H a negative one,

\mathrm{IRR} \approx L + \frac{\mathrm{NPV}_L}{\mathrm{NPV}_L - \mathrm{NPV}_H}\,(H - L)

Example (Tk 100,000 now; Tk 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 in years 1 to 3; r = 10\%):

YearNet flow (Tk)Factor at 10%PV (Tk)
0-100{,}0001.0000-100{,}000
140,0000.909136,364
250,0000.826441,322
360,0000.751345,079

NPV = Tk 22,765 and BCR = 122,765/100,000 = 1.23. NPV is +Tk 2,778 at 20% and -Tk 5,280 at 25%, so IRR \approx 20 + 2{,}778/8{,}058 \times 5 = 21.7\% (exactly 21.6%). Accept on all three.
pts: Basis: flows in different years made comparable by discounting, PV = FV/(1+r)^t
NPV defined as PV(B) - PV(C), with the formula \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t and its terms
NPV rule: accept if positive; NPV is the value added in taka; NPV = 0 means it earns exactly r
BCR defined as PV(B)/PV(C), accept if above 1
BCR > 1 exactly when NPV > 0; BCR is benefit per taka, NPV total value
IRR defined as the discount rate at which NPV = 0, accept if above the required rate
IRR found by trial and the interpolation formula, or as the zero crossing of the NPV profile
Notes that NPV is the primary criterion, with BCR and IRR as supporting measures
3a.src: CBA exam note, pp 3-9, 18; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, pp 1-2; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts III-V and VII
3a.watch:
• "Define" asks for the meaning, the formula and the rule for each; the example is support and earns no marks of its own.
  • In the interpolation, use the absolute value of the negative NPV: 2{,}778 + 5{,}280 = 8{,}058. Interpolation slightly overstates the IRR (21.7% against the exact 21.6%).
  • A project with NPV exactly zero is not "earning nothing": it earns the discount rate.

3b.html:
Given: NPV = Tk 1,087,392.40 lakh, BCR = 1.275, IRR = 45.37%.

  • NPV is positive. Discounted benefits exceed discounted costs by Tk 1,087,392.40 lakh (about Tk 10,874 crore) at the chosen discount rate. The project adds this net value to society, so it should be accepted.
  • BCR exceeds 1. Each Tk 1 of present-value cost returns Tk 1.275 of present-value benefit. The margin is moderate: benefits can fall about 22% (1 - 1/1.275) before the project stops paying.
  • IRR is 45.37%. The project earns 45.37% a year, far above any likely social discount rate (roughly 8 to 12% is common). NPV stays positive up to this rate, so the decision is robust to the discount rate.
  • Implied size. With \mathrm{NPV} = B - C and \mathrm{BCR} = B/C:
C = \frac{\mathrm{NPV}}{\mathrm{BCR} - 1} = \frac{1{,}087{,}392.40}{0.275} = 3{,}954{,}154\ \text{lakh Tk}, \qquad B = 1.275\,C = 5{,}041{,}547\ \text{lakh Tk}

Answer: all three criteria agree that the project is economically viable; approve it, subject to a sensitivity test on benefits and costs.
pts: NPV positive: PV of benefits exceeds PV of costs by Tk 1,087,392.40 lakh, so the project adds net value and is accepted
BCR 1.275 above 1: Tk 1.275 of PV benefit per Tk 1 of PV cost; accept
IRR 45.37% exceeds the social discount rate; NPV remains positive up to 45.37%
Gauges robustness or size: benefits may fall about 22% (costs rise 27.5%) before BCR = 1, or the implied PV of costs (about Tk 3,954,154 lakh) and benefits (about Tk 5,041,547 lakh)
Concludes that all three agree and recommends approval with sensitivity analysis
3b.src: Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts IV, V, VII and X; CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Standard textbook treatment
3b.watch:
• Lakh taka is the unit: Tk 1,087,392.40 lakh is Tk 10,874 crore, not Tk 1.09 million.
  • PV(C) = \mathrm{NPV}/(\mathrm{BCR} - 1) holds only for the gross BCR PV(B)/PV(C) at the same discount rate as the NPV; a net BCR gives other figures.
  • A very high IRR with a modest BCR is not a contradiction. IRR is high when benefits arrive early; BCR stays low if large recurring costs sit in the denominator.
  • NPV is the main criterion for a single project; BCR and IRR support it.

4a.html:
Not necessarily. Whether rapid growth of GNI (or GNI per capita) conflicts with a more equal distribution depends on the character of growth: how it is achieved, which sectors lead and who participates.

Arguments for a conflict (the traditional view)

  • Saving: the rich save a larger share of income, so concentrating income raises saving, investment and growth (Lewis, Harrod-Domar); redistribution lowers saving.
  • Kuznets inverted U: inequality rises in early growth while a small high-wage modern sector expands, so worse distribution is the price of growth.
  • Incentives and cost: progressive taxes blunt the rewards to effort and enterprise, and poverty spending diverts funds from investment.

Arguments against

  • Credit: the poor lack collateral, so they cannot educate their children or start firms, and they have many children for old-age security.
  • The rich are not frugal: in many poor countries they spend on luxury imports, gold and property or move savings abroad (capital flight); the middle class has the highest marginal saving rate.
  • Productivity: better health, nutrition and education raise the productivity of the poor.
  • Demand: higher incomes of the poor raise demand for local necessities, creating local jobs and investment.
  • Participation: less poverty and inequality encourage participation, while extreme disparities breed conflict and rent seeking.

Evidence. Taiwan, South Korea and Costa Rica grew fast with low or falling inequality. From the 1960s to the 1990s East Asia grew 5.5% a year per head and Africa shrank 0.2%, yet both Gini coefficients stayed about the same.

Conclusion. They are not inherently conflicting: broad-based growth that invests in the poor serves both goals.
pts: Clear position: not necessarily conflicting; the character of growth decides
For: the rich save more, so inequality raises saving and investment; redistribution lowers saving
For: the Kuznets inverted U (inequality rises in early growth)
For: incentive or fiscal-cost argument (taxes and transfers reduce effort or investment)
Against: the poor lack credit and collateral, so they under-invest in education and enterprise (or high fertility)
Against: the rich in poor countries consume luxury imports or send capital abroad; middle-class saving is highest
Against: better health, nutrition and education raise the productivity of the poor
Against: rising incomes of the poor raise demand for local goods
Against: participation and social stability (or less rent seeking)
Evidence, for example East Asian growth with low inequality, or Gini unchanged despite very different growth rates
Conclusion: compatible when growth is broad-based and invests in the poor
4a.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 3, 32-33, 36-42, 55-56; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 274-284, 298-299
4a.watch:
• Give both sides before the verdict; an answer that only lists the five counter-arguments loses the "for" marks.
  • The Kuznets curve is weak evidence for a conflict: across countries it largely reflects Latin American countries being both middle-income and unequal.
  • Modern-sector enrichment growth (gains only to those already in the modern sector) is a case where growth does worsen distribution.

4b.html:
Dependence is the reliance of developing countries on rich countries' markets, capital and policies for their own growth; rich countries also hold dominance over trade, prices and finance.

Developing countries depend on rich ones for:

  • Export markets and foreign exchange: Bangladesh's garments, 84% of its exports, sell mainly to the EU and USA.
  • Finance: aid, loans and foreign investment, and the debt that follows.
  • Technology, skills and policy: machinery, training, and IMF or World Bank conditions and advice.

Rich countries depend on developing ones for:

  • Raw materials and energy: oil, gas, cobalt, rare earths.
  • Cheap manufactures and supply chains: garments, electronics, parts.
  • Markets and profits for their goods, capital and multinationals.
  • Migrant labour and global public goods such as climate stability and disease control.

So the relationship is interdependence, but unequal: the poor depend more and have less bargaining power.
pts: Defines dependence (reliance on rich-country markets, capital and policies), with dominance
Developing countries depend on rich export markets, with an example (garments to the EU and USA)
Developing countries depend on aid, loans or foreign investment
Developing countries depend on rich-country technology, skills or policy advice and conditions
Opposite: rich countries need raw materials and energy
Opposite: rich countries rely on cheap manufactures and supply chains
Opposite: developing countries are markets and a source of profits
Opposite: migrant labour or global public goods such as climate and health
Concludes that the relationship is interdependence, but unequal
4b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slide 30; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 170-171, 174, 185; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 6
4b.watch:
• Half the marks are for "the opposite": give at least three ways rich countries depend on developing ones.
  • Marks: printed as 8 1/3; the points total 8.5.

5b.html:
Planning is the deliberate effort of a government to choose social objectives, set quantitative targets for a given period, and organise resources and policies to reach them; the plan is the document that states the targets and the strategy.

Steps of planning

  1. Survey of resources and the present situation (output, saving, labour, foreign exchange, problems).
  2. Objectives and priorities: growth, jobs, poverty reduction, regional balance.
  3. Consistent targets: for example the investment rate needed for the growth target, I/Y = c\,g.
  4. Formulation in three stages: aggregate (macro model), sectoral (allocation among sectors) and project (cost-benefit selection).
  5. Financing and approval: saving, taxes and foreign aid; approval by the top economic body (in Bangladesh, the National Economic Council).
  6. Implementation through annual development programmes, the budget and policies.
  7. Monitoring, evaluation and revision, which feed the next plan.

Example: Bangladesh's five-year plans follow these steps, prepared by the Planning Commission and carried out through each year's Annual Development Programme.
pts: Defines planning: objectives, quantitative targets for a period, and organised means to reach them
Survey of resources and the present situation
Objectives and priorities
Consistent quantitative targets
Formulation in aggregate, sectoral and project stages
Financing and approval
Implementation through annual programmes and policies
Monitoring, evaluation and revision feeding the next plan
5b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 600, 603-604, 610-611; Standard textbook treatment
5b.watch:
• Textbooks give five to eight steps; any sensible sequence from survey to monitoring earns full credit.
  • The course has no planning slides; this follows Todaro section 11.2-11.3. The fuller answer with a worked real-life example is HUM-2022-23 Q6b.

6a.html:
The Lewis two-sector model (W. Arthur Lewis, 1954) explains development as the transfer of surplus labour from the traditional agricultural sector to the modern industrial sector, whose growth absorbs that labour, industrialises the economy and makes growth self-sustaining.

Assumptions about the two sectors

  • Traditional sector: overpopulated subsistence farming with fixed land and technology. There is surplus labour: the marginal product of labour, MP_{LA}, is zero, so workers can be withdrawn without losing output. Families share output equally, so the rural income W_A equals the average product, TP_A/L_A.
  • Modern sector: urban industry with competitive, profit-maximising employers, who hire until the marginal product of labour equals the wage; the MP_{LM} curve is therefore the labour demand curve.

The growth mechanism

  1. Unlimited labour supply. The urban wage W_M is fixed at a premium over W_A to cover the cost of moving. Because surplus workers earn only W_A on the farm, industry can hire any number at W_M: the supply curve W_M S_L is flat.
  2. Profits. With capital K_{M1}, demand D_1 meets supply at F, employing L_1. Output is the area 0D_1FL_1; workers get 0W_MFL_1 and capitalists keep the profit W_MD_1F.
  3. Reinvestment. Capitalists reinvest all profits, so capital rises to K_{M2}, the marginal product of labour rises and demand shifts out to D_2; employment grows to L_2 at the same wage. Bigger profits are reinvested again (D_3, L_3): growth feeds itself.
  4. Turning point. Once the surplus is absorbed, further withdrawals cut farm output; the supply curve turns upward and real wages rise (the Lewis turning point).

Outcome: the economy's structure shifts from rural agriculture to urban industry, at a speed set by the rate of capital accumulation in the modern sector. The model fits the West's history and China's growth.
pts: States the model: surplus labour transferred from traditional agriculture to a growing modern industrial sector
Explains surplus labour: MP_{LA} = 0, so labour can leave agriculture without loss of output
Rural wage W_A set by the average product because output is shared, not by the marginal product
Explains the unlimited (horizontal) labour supply at a fixed urban wage W_M above W_A
Employment where MP_{LM} = W_M (in words or on a diagram), with output split into wages and profits
Explains reinvestment of all profits: capital rises, labour demand shifts out, employment grows at a constant wage, so growth is self-sustaining
Lewis turning point: once the surplus is absorbed the supply curve rises and wages increase
Outcome: structural transformation from agriculture to industry, paced by capital accumulation
6a.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 22-26; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 163-166
6a.watch:
• "Explain" wants the reasons: why supply is flat (zero rural marginal product, wage above rural income) and why growth continues (profits reinvested).
  • The figure is the clearest way to show the mechanism, but the marks are for the reasoning, in words or on the diagram.
  • Keep average and marginal product apart: rural income is the average product; the surplus is defined by a zero marginal product.

6b.html:
Rostow's model (1960) says every country passes through five stages: traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity and high mass consumption (a sixth, the search for quality, was added in 1971). Take-off comes from a sharp rise in saving and investment.

My view: partly relevant.

Still relevant

  • Saving and investment do drive growth (Harrod-Domar, g = s/c): South Korea's investment rose from 15% of GNI in 1965 to 37% in 1990.
  • Structural change from agriculture to industry, led by key sectors (garments in Bangladesh), is still observed.

Limited

  • Investment is necessary, not sufficient: the Marshall Plan worked in Europe because institutions, skills and markets existed; many poor countries lack them.
  • Not one linear path: stages are skipped or merged, and their boundaries are vague.
  • It ignores international constraints, inequality and the environment.

Conclusion: useful as a description and a reminder that investment matters, but not a blueprint for development today.
pts: States the model and names the five stages in order
Clear position with reasons ("relevant", "not relevant" or "partly" all earn this if argued)
Relevance: saving and investment drive growth, with an example or the Harrod-Domar link
Relevance: structural change and leading sectors still observed
Limitation: investment necessary but not sufficient (Marshall Plan contrast; institutions and skills)
Limitation: single linear path; stages skipped, merged or vague
Limitation: ignores international constraints, inequality or the environment
Conclusion consistent with the position
6b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 3-7, 19-21; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 159, 162-163, 181
6b.watch:
• Marks: printed as 8 1/3; the points total 8.5.
  • Do not spend the answer describing the stages; the question asks whether the model is relevant.

7a.html:
Foreign currency reserves are the foreign assets (mainly US dollars) that the central bank holds to pay for imports and debt and to steady the exchange rate; a common rule of adequacy is at least three months of imports.

The crisis. Bangladesh Bank's gross reserves peaked at about USD 48 billion (August 2021) and fell to about USD 26.8 billion by June 2024 (about USD 21 to 22 billion by the IMF's BPM6 count): a dollar shortage, import curbs and a falling taka.

Causes

  1. Import surge after COVID-19: imports exceeded USD 80 billion in FY2021-22, a record current-account deficit of about USD 18 billion.
  2. 2022 price shock: the Russia-Ukraine war raised fuel, LNG, fertiliser, wheat and edible-oil prices.
  3. Strong dollar: US rate rises pulled capital out; short-term trade credit was not rolled over.
  4. Exchange-rate policy: the taka was held near Tk 86 per USD with multiple rates; overvaluation encouraged imports and discouraged formal inflows, and the move to about Tk 110 to 120 came late.
  5. Remittances diverted to hundi: with the kerb rate above the official rate, formal remittances fell from about USD 24.8 billion (FY2020-21, boosted by COVID travel limits) to about USD 21.0 billion (FY2021-22).
  6. Capital flight: over-invoiced imports, unrepatriated export earnings and money laundering.
  7. Structural weakness: RMG-dependent exports, small FDI, rising repayments of megaproject and private loans.
  8. Running reserves down: Bangladesh Bank sold dollars (more than USD 13 billion in FY2022-23) to defend the taka, and the gross figure had counted loans to exporters from the Export Development Fund.

Conclusion: an external price shock met a held-down exchange rate, weak governance of capital flows and a narrow export base; selling reserves bought time but deepened the loss.
pts: Defines foreign currency reserves and their use (imports, debt, exchange-rate stability)
Describes the fall: from about USD 48 billion (2021) to about USD 20 to 27 billion (2023 to 2024)
Post-COVID import surge and the 2022 commodity price shock widened the current-account deficit
Strong dollar after US rate rises: capital outflow or non-rollover of short-term credit
Overvalued, rigid exchange rate with multiple rates, adjusted late
Remittances diverted to hundi because of the gap between kerb and official rates
Capital flight, money laundering or trade misinvoicing
Narrow export base, low FDI or rising external debt repayments
Central-bank dollar sales or inflated gross accounting (EDF, BPM6) ran reserves down
Concludes that external shocks combined with domestic policy and governance failures
7a.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slide 6; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 802-803, 810-812; Standard textbook treatment
7a.watch:
• The paper is from the 2020-21 session but was sat later; "recent" means the 2022 to 2024 crisis. Figures other than the slide's are Bangladesh Bank and press data quoted from memory: write "about" and the year; the June 2024 value of USD 26,815 million is hum-dim slide 6, and quoting it, or any reasonable recent value, earns the same credit.
  • Gross and BPM6 reserves differ by several billion dollars: BPM6 (the IMF's balance-of-payments manual) excludes the Export Development Fund and other non-liquid claims. Name the measure when you quote a number.
  • Credit any sound cause with a reason; a list of labels without the mechanism earns little.

7b.html:
Short run (stop the drain)

  1. Market-based, unified exchange rate (for example a crawling peg), so formal remittance and export channels pay as well as hundi.
  2. Curb non-essential imports (higher LC margins on luxuries) and tighten monetary policy to cut import demand and inflation.
  3. Stop leakages: check invoice prices, enforce repatriation of export proceeds, act against hundi and laundering.
  4. Official financing: IMF, World Bank and ADB support; defer import-heavy projects that are not urgent.

Long run (raise dollar inflows for good)

  1. Diversify exports beyond RMG: leather, pharmaceuticals, light engineering, agro-processing, ICT.
  2. Attract FDI through working economic zones and a stable policy regime.
  3. Raise remittances by skilled migration and cheaper formal channels; cut energy imports through gas exploration and renewables.
  4. Governance and prudent borrowing: banking reform, concessional loans only for projects that earn or save foreign exchange.

Conclusion: short-run measures stabilise reserves; only a wider export and investment base keeps them adequate.
pts: Short run: market-based or unified exchange rate to restore formal remittance and export inflows
Short run: import restrictions or tighter monetary policy
Short run: action against hundi, misinvoicing or capital flight, or IMF and multilateral support
Long run: export diversification beyond RMG
Long run: attract FDI through economic zones and a better investment climate
Long run: raise remittances or cut energy import dependence
Long run: governance, banking reform and prudent, concessional borrowing
7b.src: Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slide 12; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 802-803, 810-812; Standard textbook treatment
7b.watch:
• Keep the two horizons separate: the question asks for both, and a student who mixes them loses the structure the examiner looks for.
  • Several of these were actually adopted in 2022 to 2024 (LC margins, IMF programme of about USD 4.7 billion in 2023, the crawling peg of May 2024); citing them as evidence is good.
  • Import curbs are a stopgap: if held long they starve industry of inputs and slow exports.

8a.html:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 global goals with 169 targets, adopted by the UN in September 2015 to be achieved by 2030. They replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015).

Principles: universality (they apply to every country), integration (all goals together, as they interact) and transformation (not piecemeal steps).

The goals fall under People (1 no poverty, 2 zero hunger, 3 health, 4 education, 5 gender equality), Prosperity (7 energy, 8 decent work, 9 industry, 10 inequality, 11 cities), Planet (6 water, 12 consumption, 13 climate, 14 oceans, 15 land), Peace (16) and Partnership (17). They aim to end poverty rather than halve it.

Bangladesh ranks 114th of 167 on the 2025 SDG Index (score 63.9), with 20.8% of targets on track.
pts: Defines the SDGs: 17 goals, 169 targets, UN 2015, deadline 2030, successors of the MDGs
States the principles: universality, integration and transformation
Names the goals, grouped or listed (at least ten goals correctly)
Notes a difference from the MDGs (end rather than halve poverty, universal coverage, inequality and institutions added)
Gives Bangladesh's status or a key challenge (rank 114, 20.8% of targets on track, financing gap)

8b.html:
Lorenz curve. A graph of the size distribution of income: with people ranked from poorest to richest, the cumulative percentage of income against the cumulative percentage of population. The diagonal is the line of perfect equality; the more the curve bows below it, the more unequal the distribution. In Table 5.1 the bottom 50% receives 19.8% of income.

Gini coefficient. A summary measure of the Lorenz curve: the area between the diagonal and the curve divided by the whole triangle under the diagonal, G = A/(A+B). It ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality); unequal countries lie near 0.50 to 0.70, equal ones near 0.20 to 0.35. Table 5.1 gives 0.44; Bangladesh 0.32 (2010).

Use. A Lorenz curve wholly above another is more equal; crossing curves are ambiguous. The Gini satisfies anonymity, scale and population independence and the transfer principle.
pts: Lorenz curve axes: cumulative % of population (ranked) and cumulative % of income
Diagonal = perfect equality; greater bow = greater inequality
Gini = A/(A+B), the area between the diagonal and the curve over the triangle
Range 0 to 1 with typical values or an example
Lorenz criterion: a higher curve is more equal; crossing curves are ambiguous
Gini meets anonymity, scale independence, population independence and the transfer principle

8c.html:
Balanced growth (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan): invest simultaneously in many complementary industries, and in agriculture and industry together. The reason is the small market: one factory cannot sell to poor consumers, but many factories become each other's customers, breaking the vicious circle of poverty on the demand side. Criticism: it needs capital, skills and administrative capacity a poor country lacks, and it ignores trade.

Unbalanced growth (Hirschman, 1958): invest first in a few key sectors with the strongest backward and forward linkages. The resulting shortages and surpluses send profit signals that induce investment in lagging sectors: growth as a "chain of disequilibria", economising on scarce decision-making ability. The path runs through excess social overhead capital (SOC: infrastructure first) or its shortage (factories first). Criticism: bottlenecks, inflation, regional inequality.

Bangladesh: RMG-led growth with its linkages is close to unbalanced growth.
pts: Balanced growth: simultaneous investment in many complementary sectors (Nurkse, Rosenstein-Rodan)
Its rationale: small market size; sectors create demand for each other, breaking the vicious circle
A criticism of balanced growth: resources and capacity lacking, or neglect of trade
Unbalanced growth: deliberate investment in key sectors with strongest linkages (Hirschman)
Its mechanism: imbalances create pressures and signals that induce investment, a chain of disequilibria (SOC or DPA path)
A criticism of unbalanced growth: bottlenecks, inflation or regional inequality
A Bangladesh example or a one-line contrast of the two

8d.html:
Foreign aid is the transfer of official grants and concessional loans (softer than market terms) to promote development, bilaterally (Japan, China, Russia, India) or through agencies such as the World Bank and ADB.

Role in Bangladesh

  • Two gaps: aid supplemented scarce saving and foreign exchange for reconstruction, food imports and investment.
  • Infrastructure: Jamuna Bridge, power plants, Dhaka Metro Rail (Japan), Rooppur nuclear plant (Russia).
  • Human development: immunisation, family planning (fertility from about 6 to 2.17), school stipends, cyclone shelters, early NGO support (BRAC).

Changing pattern: aid fell from roughly 6 to 10% of GNI in the 1970s and 1980s to about 1 to 1.5% now, though disbursement is still large (about USD 10 billion in FY2021-22); loans have replaced grants.

Problems: tying, conditions, slow disbursement, leakage and rising debt service; the Padma Bridge was self-financed after the World Bank withdrew.

Conclusion: aid is now a supplement, not the engine of development.
pts: Defines foreign aid: official grants and concessional loans, bilateral or multilateral
Fills the saving and foreign-exchange gaps
Infrastructure role with a named Bangladesh project
Human development role: health, family planning, education, disaster preparedness or NGOs
Changing pattern: falling dependence on aid relative to GNI (no exact figure needed), or the shift from grants to loans
Problems (tying, conditions, slow use, leakage or debt service) and a conclusion that aid is now a supplement
